The city had a department for everything, including things that had stopped existing.

There was an Office of Removed Trees, where the clerks kept rings of old trunks pressed between glass. There was a Bureau of Interrupted Songs, staffed mostly by people who hummed while eating. And beneath the courthouse, down a stairway that smelled of wet wool, was the Department of Lost Mornings.

Mara found it on a Thursday, though the morning she had lost belonged to a Tuesday seventeen years earlier.

She had been nine. Her father had promised to teach her how to whistle with a blade of grass. That was all she remembered: his hands held close to her face, the green strip between his thumbs, his instruction to blow harder.

Then came the telephone call.

After that, whenever she recalled the day, it began with the call. Her father answering it. His shoulders settling into a shape she had never seen before. The drive to the hospital. Her mother’s coat folded over a chair.

The grass was still there somewhere. She was certain of it.

At the department’s front desk, an elderly man was repairing a stapler.

“I’m looking for a morning,” she said.

“Aren’t we all.”

He did not look up.

“I mean a particular one.”

“That narrows it considerably.”

He gave her a form with seven boxes.

Date. Approximate duration. Weather. Persons present. Reason for loss. Intended use upon recovery. Signature.

Under *Reason for loss*, Mara wrote: *Something happened afterward.*

The clerk read this and nodded.

“Most common cause.”

He led her through a door into a room much larger than the building above it. Shelves rose into dimness. On them stood thousands of glass jars, each holding a small quantity of light.

Some were pale and gray. Others burned gold. One contained a furious pink flicker.

“Sunrise over a laundromat,” the clerk said, noticing her glance. “Unexpectedly popular.”

“People lose that?”

“People lose everything.”

They stopped at a shelf marked with the year she had given.

The clerk ran one finger along the labels.

“Tuesday. Nine years old. Grass instruction. Here.”

The jar was smaller than she expected. About the size of one used for mustard.

Inside, the light was green.

“What do I do?”

“Open it.”

“Here?”

“Unless you’d prefer to take it home. But there is one thing.”

She waited.

“It won’t change anything that happened later.”

“I know.”

“Most people say that.”

“I do know.”

He handed her the jar and withdrew to his desk.

Mara sat on a wooden stool. The lid resisted, then gave with a soft click.

There was no flash.

She was simply in the garden.

The grass was damp through her trousers. Her father sat cross-legged beside her in the old blue shirt with a missing button. There was soil beneath one of his fingernails. A fly landed on his knee and departed.

“No, like this,” he said.

He stretched the blade between his thumbs. Blew. A thin, rude shriek cut through the air.

Mara laughed.

The sound startled her more than the garden had.

For seventeen years she had remembered herself as a child waiting unknowingly for disaster. Here she was merely laughing at a ridiculous noise.

Her father selected another blade.

“Your turn.”

“I can’t.”

“You haven’t tried.”

“I did.”

“You breathed on it. That’s different.”

She pressed her thumbs together. The blade slipped.

He waited while she tried again.

From inside the house came the clatter of a spoon dropped on the kitchen tiles.

Her mother.

Not a coat over a chair. Not the pale rectangle of a hospital pillow. Her mother, mildly annoyed with a spoon.

Mara turned toward the open back door.

“Don’t go wandering,” her father said. “You’ve nearly got it.”

She wanted to stand. To run inside. To say something immense and impossible.

Instead she stayed.

The grass squealed between her hands.

“There,” he said, smiling. “See?”

The morning ended.

She was back on the stool, holding an empty jar.

For a long time she listened to the clerk working on his stapler. Metal clicked against metal. Somewhere among the shelves, someone sneezed.

Finally she stood.

“Can I come again?”

“Of course.”

“For the same morning?”

The clerk shook his head.

“Once returned, they don’t belong to us.”

She looked into the jar. A drop of moisture clung to the bottom.

“Will I remember it?”

“Not perfectly.”

That seemed unfair. Then it seemed ordinary.

At the door, she asked, “Why are they in jars?”

The clerk tested the stapler on a scrap of paper.

“What would you put them in?”

Outside, the city was having an unremarkable afternoon. A delivery cyclist argued with a taxi driver. Rain gathered in the seams of the pavement. Someone had left a chair beside a rubbish bin, though the chair appeared perfectly good.

Mara walked to the little park behind the library.

For years she had told the story of her mother’s death beginning with the telephone. She had gone back over the words her father used, trying to remember which came first, as though the right order might make them easier to hear.

Now she could also remember the missing button on his shirt.

At the edge of the path, she found a long blade of grass.

She wiped it on her sleeve and placed it between her thumbs. She blew until her head felt light. Nothing happened.

A boy passing with his grandmother stopped to watch.

“You’re doing it wrong,” he said.

“I know.”

“You have to make a little hole.”

She adjusted her hands.

The grass gave a sharp, embarrassing cry.

The boy grinned. His grandmother pulled gently on his hand, and they continued down the path.

Mara chose another blade.
